utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-04-75-T, the Prosecutor versus Goran Hadzic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. May we have the appearances, please, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For the Prosecution this morning, Alex Demirdjian with Lisa Biersay; our case manager, Thomas Laugel; and our legal intern, Agnes Bugaj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. For the Defence, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For the Defence of Goran Hadzic, Zoran Zivanovic and Christopher Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. There is a short oral ruling I could deal with. The Trial Chamber is seized of a Prosecution motion to replace the translation of Exhibit P1004 with a corrected version. The Defence does not object. The Chamber hereby grants the request and directs the Registrar to take the appropriate measures to implement this decision. And if there is nothing else, the witness may be brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Witness. Could you tell us your name, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Reynaud Theunens, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You are about to read the solemn declaration, by which witnesses commit themselves to tell the truth. I need to point out to you, as you probably know, that you are exposing yourself to the penalties of perjury should you give untruthful information to the Tribunal. Would you now please read the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, I wouldn't ask for your ethnicity, as we often do for people -- for witnesses from the region, but out of personal curiosity, are you a native French speaker or a native Dutch speaker?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am a native Dutch speaker but as an officer in the military I also acquired I think a decent knowledge of French.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Demirdjian, your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Theunens.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Demirdjian.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Before I begin, am I correct in thinking that you have a copy of your amalgamated report in a binder before you?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Perfect. Thank you. And I'd like to -- before I begin, I would just like to remind you and myself that considering that we both speak the same language, I'd like to make sure that we make pauses between answers and questions. First of all, could I ask that we have 65 ter 3044 on the screen, which is Mr. Theunens' resume. And that's at tab 668. And while that is being brought up, Mr. Theunens, could I ask you to briefly give the Trial Chamber your educational background, please.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: I attended military academy in Belgium from August 1993 -- 1983, I'm sorry, until December 1987, and I obtained a degree of masters in social and military sciences. After that, I attended armour school, I attended trainings abroad in intelligence as well as in peacekeeping, I mean you can find it in the resume. And in 1997 I attended the brigade-level staff course in Belgium.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. What is your current occupation?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, since April 2009 I'm chief of the joint mission analysis centre in the United Nations interim force in Lebanon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And prior to that, it is correct that you were employed at the ICTY?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours. From July 2001 until April 2009 I worked as an information analyst or intelligence analyst military in the Office of the Prosecutor at the ICTY.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And during your tenure at the ICTY, did you specialise on a particular area?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Basically the job of an intelligence analyst military consists of reviewing military documents in order, in my case, to identify chains of command, chains of command and reporting. I think initially I worked mainly on cases involving Serb perpetrators in Croatia. As I indicated, I mean, identifying chains of command and of reporting, that concerned predominantly relations between the JNA, the Territorial Defence, and then groups which were identified as paramilitaries or as volunteers. I also looked into issues of support, I mean combat support, logistics, personnel, and so on. And later on, I mean, I didn't work on the investigation, but I also testified in a case involving a Croatian perpetrator, i.e., or Croatian perpetrators, General Gotovina, General Markac, I think that was in 2009. I didn't participate in investigation, but I prepared a similar report as I did for this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, before we move on through these issues, could you give the Trial Chamber a brief overview of your professional background before joining the ICTY in 2002 -- 2001.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, as -- after armour school, as any young officer in the armour -- in the Belgian -- sorry, it has to be armour school in the transcript. I joined the 2nd Guides Regiment in Germany, the Belgian armed forces in Germany where I worked as a platoon commander, sometimes as a second in command of a company, and then as a personnel officer. After that, I returned to military academy as an instructor and a promotion commander for a year. And then on my own request I changed assignment and I was moved to the Ministry of Defence where I worked as an intelligence analyst on the Balkans, I mean this was in September 1992 and basically I stayed there in similar assignments until July 2001 when I left the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, as part of your work as of September 1992, is it correct to say that you were sent to the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours. I participated in three peacekeeping operations. The first one was in December 1994 till September 1995, where I worked as an information analyst -- I'm sorry, military information officer, I'm sorry, military information officer in the headquarters of UNPROFOR/UNPF in Zagreb which was the headquarters covering all UN peacekeeping operations in the former Yugoslavia at that time. From July 1996 until May 1997 I had a similar -- held a similar position in the UNTAES headquarters of the United Nations Transitional Administration Eastern Slavonia headquartered in Vukovar. And then December 1999 until I think that was also May 2000, I was a chief of a national intelligence cell in the SFOR, the stability force headquarters Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Mr. Theunens. I'd like to move on to your -- the report that was prepared for the purposes of this case. Now, is it correct to say that the report that you have --

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Well, actually, sorry, Your Honours, before I move on. The resume is not a document in the report. Might I ask to tender that, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Shall be assigned Exhibit P1682. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And while we're dealing with the report, could we display the cover page of the report which is 65 ter 5988, please. Mr. Theunens, in -- with respect to the report that we have for this case, it is correct to say this is an amalgamated report composed of various parts of previous reports you had prepared at the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honours. And if need, I can explain what that is a reason -- I mean, how this happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, we will get into that.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Oh, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, first of all, could you tell the Court which of your previous reports were used to create the amalgamated report we have here?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, this report -- I mean amalgamated report includes elements of reports I drafted for the Karadzic case; Martic case; Stanisic/Simatovic; Vukovar three, or Mrksic, Sljivancanin, and Radic; and the Seselj case. I think that covers all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes. And could you tell us briefly how this report was put together?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yesterday, basically, I looked back at my notes and -- because since I work in Lebanon I've returned to the ICTY a few times. And if my recollection is correct, I came back in March 2012 to work on a report for the Mladic case and I also reviewed -- I was contacted by the Hadzic Prosecution team and I looked at -- I mean my previous reports, the ones I mentioned which covered related issues, but I also identified additional issues I would like to cover in my Hadzic report, and of course that required certain documents. And it was my understanding that these documents - and these were mainly documents concerning or covering the relations between the JNA and the civilian authorities - that there were no additional documents available compared to what was available to me and actually what I had requested at the time I was working on the Vukovar case. When I say I had requested, that was requested through RFAs, requests for assistance to the Government of the Republic of Serbia. And so my conclusion to the Prosecution was that, actually, there was not much to add at that stage because in my view important documents were lacking. So it was decided to prepare a kind of a preliminary, what I would call a cut/paste of the reports that I mentioned, focusing on issues that I believed to be relevant for the Hadzic case. My next trip to The Hague may have been in summer 2012. I don't recall exactly when, but it was not for this case. It may have been for Mladic again. But in any event, I was informed when I came then for a third time but actually a second time for Hadzic, I believe that was in September/October 2012, I was informed that additional documents had been made available and including translations. So I was given the opportunity to review these documents and I considered that these were really -- I mean key documents. And I decided to prepare a new report basically reducing what was -- had become -- I mean the amalgamated report, i.e., the cut-and-paste had been transformed into an amalgamated report. I had -- and my new report would thus only include the relevant sections of the amalgamated report in a kind of reader-friendly structure and layout. In addition, a section that covered -- that reviewed the new documents. With "new documents," I mean by that documents on operational group south -- sorry, operational group north, other JNA elements in Baranja in the northern part of Eastern Slavonia as well as relations between them and the authorities of the SAO/SBWS, as well as what I considered the most important relations between the JNA and the SAO/SBWS authorities after November and more specifically after the 20th of November, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, with respect to the report we have before us here, you mentioned that these were, as you put it a cut and paste from previous reports. Could you tell us how the report -- the amalgamated report we have before us, how were the portions selected, the portions that we have from each of the previous reports?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I selected those based on my assessment of the relevance of these portions for the Hadzic case. And, as usual, all my reports basically consist of two parts. The first part is a doctrine, I mean, the general legal framework as it existed in SFRY and then FRY together with the main aspects of the JNA's or the VJ's military doctrine. And that I took from the Karadzic report because that was at that stage my last report on -- for the ICTY. And then for the second part, which discusses the operations or the actual operations, I looked at work I had done or reports I had submitted in the Martic case, Vukovar three, Seselj, and Stanisic/Simatovic, and I had identified those elements and those sections I considered relevant and communicated -- I mean the page numbers to the OTP who then put it all together in one document. They showed that to me or they sent it to me, asking whether that was what I -- whether it corresponded with what I had selected. I said yes. And this is how the amalgamated report was then, yeah, compiled.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I'd like us to turn to the issue of the focus of your analysis in this report, and first perhaps we could -- I could ask you about the sources that you have used in the past when creating these reports.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the choice of sources is obviously closely related to the methodology I apply, where basically when selecting sources two criteria apply, i.e., the reliability of the source and the credibility of the information. In relation to the reliability of the source, in this cases we -- I mean, we are basically talking about activities of states, state authorities or entity -- authorities of entities as well as of military structures. So the most obvious choice is to take original documents issued by these state authorities or authorities or entities or military authorities, and that covers a wide range going from the constitution to military regulations, military orders, situation reports, information or intelligence reports, but I would obviously, I mean, focus -- when I select these documents, I apply the criteria in a sense I would look at what is, for example, the relation between the entity -- no, between the organisation that issued the document and the events described in the document. And it would of course in this context make more sense to use an order signed by the commander of OG South, I mean, when discussing the operations of OG South than, for example, take a Croatian newspaper article, I mean just to give you one example. I was in I think an enormous privilege also compared to my previous work, that in the OTP there is an enormous amount of original documents issued by the parties. So in this case I would look at documents from the JNA, the SAO Krajina, TO, SAO SBWS TO, the SVK, as well as documents issued by the SFRY Presidency, for example, FRY Presidency, and related.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. And what views have you developed over the course of the preparation of your reports with respect to the authenticity of the documents you've reviewed?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, during the time I worked at the ICTY, I mean at the OTP between 2001 and 2009, I -- I think I was also privileged to be involved in a number of witness interviews, whereby -- I mean, those witnesses were mainly JNA officers. So we would use some of these documents, depending of the case, and submit them to them and -- obviously we would ask the witnesses whether this document was authentic. I mean, in many cases they had signed the document. So that's one way of authenticating. We also looked at the original of the document. Most of these documents -- I mean, there is two -- two of -- yeah, two big categories. There is a group of documents that have been obtained through searches conducted by ICTY/OTP personnel of various archives. I myself during the time I was here I was involved in searching archives of the SVK that were -- had been captured by or seized by the Croatian armed forces during Operation Storm in August 1995 and I went to state archives in Zagreb and Sisak with investigators and other analysts and we reviewed these documents. And again, these documents were then shown to witnesses, and these were SVK documents, and we showed them to former SVK officers in order to authenticate them. A second group of documents that were provided by the Government of FRY and subsequently the Government of Serbia. And also there, when possible, we tried to show them to witnesses or compare them with other documents, I mean the layout, signatures, and so on, and I'm confident that the documents I have used in my report and is for sure in the amalgamated report because they have also been used in other cases and no objections have been formulated there as to their authenticity that these documents I have used are authentic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. Now, a moment ago you mentioned that after the filing of your report last summer you were given an opportunity in September to look at documents that were obtained from the Government of Serbia. Just to be clear, were these documents received after the filing of your report?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: I mean, I saw them after the filing of the report and also the translation. I'm not sure when the OTP received them. I think they received them afterwards, I'm not sure, but as far as the translations and actual -- I mean, the time they were shown to me, that was after July -- or I was notified after July and then we arranged a trip for September/October.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And during your trip during September/October, you were given an opportunity to review the translations of the documents?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. We will deal with those at a later stage. I would like us to turn to page 2 of your report, so we can briefly look at the table of contents. And here what we see on -- well, we'll see it in a minute on the screen - yes - if we could zoom in a little bit. Thank you. Yeah. Just to briefly explain this to the Trial Chamber, we see here "report for case IT 95-5/18." Could you tell us what that refers to?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: This -- I mean, the background part comes from the report for the Karadzic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And -- now, when you selected portions from the five previous cases, is it correct to say that these portions were kept together, meaning that all the Karadzic excerpts were kept together in one section?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours, and that also explains that there is sometimes overlap, I mean not for what I would call the first part, the doctrinal background, but in the second part where we discuss, for example, the operations in Croatia or the establishment of local Serb armed forces, there may be some overlap between the different reports because these topics were discussed in different reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. So this means that essentially each excerpt follows -- one excerpt follows the other, the excerpt from the Karadzic case is followed by one from another case?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yes, they were not integrated, but they were just added one after the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And just a little note here, in some of the footnotes throughout your report, it is correct in past cases you had used 65 ter numbers and exhibit numbers; is that right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: That is correct, because it dates back from the time before e-court and in some cases we had already exhibit numbers before the report was filed which facilitated the referencing during testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: So with respect to our purposes here, should we ignore those numbers?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. Yes. Well, I'd like to move on now to the subjects that you deal with in your report, starting with the background first. If we could -- if I could take you to page 17 of your report where you deal with the SFRY armed forces. So I'd like to deal with the doctrine a little bit before we move on to the actual operations during the war. And here we see that you are dealing with the All People's Defence and the constitution. Could you tell us, first of all, what were the constituent parts of the SFRY armed forces?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the SFRY armed forces consisted of the JNA and the Territorial Defence, whereby the Territorial Defence includes all armed formations that are not part of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, you quote here Article 240 of the 1974 Constitution and it indicates here that any citizen who takes part in resisting aggression towards the country is a member of the armed forces of the SFRY. Now, I believe you highlight this, and this is on page 18, that this has implications with respect to command responsibility. Could you expand a little bit on this?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. By becoming a member of the armed forces of the SFRY, the individual is also subject to all the legislation and regulations that apply to the armed forces, and for the commander by using these individuals they -- I mean, it's -- it's a basic principle of command responsibility, they will also become responsible for their activities by admitting them in the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. Now -- well, on the screen I see that in the English version we would have had to scroll to the bottom of the page to see the excerpt we were discussing. Yes, I think it follows on the following page, that's the excerpt I just read.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, at page 20 of your report you explain that the JNA is the core of the Yugoslav armed forces and that a second component that you just told us was the Territorial Defence. Are there significant differences between the JNA and the TO?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I mean, in a nutshell, the JNA covers all the SFRY republics and autonomous regions. The TO is organised by republic or autonomous region. The JNA was -- I mean, in layman's term was a professional armed force and if there were conscripts, of course, but was -- also had heavy weapons, whereas the TO, which was organised by the republics, did not have heavy weapons. And basically the TO concept was introduced by Tito in 1968, whereas the other JNA was established much earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. Now, can you explain to the Judges the structure of the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: As I mentioned, the TO was organised by republic and by autonomous region, whereas the JNA was an army that covered the whole of SFRY and was consisting at that time, for example, in -- for military districts, whereby most military districts covered the territory of more than one republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And what implication did that have, the fact that the TO was organised by republic?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: That -- it meant that the republics were responsible for organising and equipping the TO, and I haven't gone in detail in that -- in my report, but many people at the time, and especially after the death of Tito and when some republics express aspirations for a weakening of central authority or even independence, then a number of -- I mean, some officers in the JNA or Yugoslav officers, they see -- they feel that the TO in those republics that seek independence could develop into an republican armed force or a republican army.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. And in each republic, who does the TO -- who is it responsible to, who does it report to?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: We would have to look at the specific regulations, but the ones I reviewed show that there is a commander of the TO who is responsible for planning, organising, training, manning, I mean it's more like a management role. And he responds to the -- or she -- no, he responds to the president of the republic, whereas in operations if the JNA and the TO operate together, then at least during the combat operations I have reviewed in Croatia covering the 1991 time-period, it is the JNA that is in command.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, at page 21 of your report, you refer to Article 102 of the Law on All People's Defence. This is the law that was adopted, I believe, in 1983; is that right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: It's 1982, Your Honours, and I mean it confirms what I said earlier, also that the Territorial Defence comprises all armed formations that are not included in the JNA or the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, I'd like to refer exactly to that second paragraph of Article 102 which we have on the screen. For purposes of this case it's Exhibit L10 which is at tab 10 as well of our list. Here it reads that the: "Territorial Defence shall comprise all armed formations that are not incorporated in the Yugoslav People's Army and the police." So I'd like to ask you what are the other armed formations that this is referring to?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Well, if you ask the question in the context of the conflict of 1991, which of course happens nine years later, but there we see the appearance mainly on the Serbian side of what is described as volunteer forces, of volunteer units, others describe them as paramilitaries, but a paramilitary in the sense of groups or formations that are not foreseen by law but that function in accordance to military doctrine, i.e., they have a military -- they try to adopt a military structure or they carry out activities that -- of a military nature. So we see appearance of these groups, and I assume we will go into that. And they're often identified in military documents as TO detachments, whereas, in fact, they have nothing to do with the TO. But in order to give them -- I mean, my conclusion is in order to give them a bit of a legal or to legalise them and to regulate their presence and their participation in the operations, they are identified as TO detachments.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, we will come to that a little bit later, but on the next page, page 22 of your report, you do deal with the concept of volunteers, which appears to be provided by the law. Could you perhaps summarise the concept itself of a volunteer to the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. And also to clarify my previous answer, Article 119 of the 1982 All People's Defence law refers to individual volunteers, whereby volunteers are people -- are identified as or defined as people who have no military obligations. The volunteer groups I spoke about in my previous answer -- I actually -- I mean, as I said "groups, these -- the volunteers, they are not individuals but they operate in one single group. And they also include people with military obligations who - again this is discussed in my report - who for mainly political reasons refuse to be part of the JNA, I mean refuse to respond to the mobilisation and other call-ups and prefer to serve in a politically or affiliated volunteer groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, we see here Article 119 that there are categories perhaps of volunteers which are persons who are not subject to military service and persons who are not conscripts.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Perhaps could you just explain to us what type of persons fit under these categories, having regard to the military service that was in place at the time?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: It could include -- it would include, for example, people who are beyond the age of call-ups, I mean, but maybe they still feel able or fit to participate in the defence of the country but they are beyond the age of being called up or maybe they have some physical shortcomings whereby they couldn't operate in a combat unit but maybe they feel they could participate in logistical support jobs, it's more in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. And on the next page at page 23 of your report, you provide -- you conclude here that the legal framework effective at the time did not foresee the establishment of volunteer formations. Could you expand on that a little bit, please.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yes, it basically comes back to what I said, I mean the law talks about individuals and these individuals were then incorporated in existing JNA or TO units, and I mean we can maybe later go into the reasons for that, why it is important not to have -- I mean from a command and control concept -- point of view, not to have separate units all with their own motivation, but instead separate volunteer units, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: But instead have them included in different groups, and also we see that in the course of -- I mean, between July 1991 and December 1991 a number of decisions are adopted by the Republic of Serbia, the SFRY armed forces Supreme Command Staff, and most importantly, the SFRY Presidency, to legalise the participation of volunteer formations into the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: In the conflict, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. We see at the bottom of that page that you also deal with the use of the police, which is provided by Article 104 of the Law on National Defence. And on the next page, which is page 24, you discuss the mission of the SFRY armed forces. In a nutshell, could you tell the Court what was the mission of the SFRY armed forces prior to the conflict?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: The mission is taken from -- as I put in the report is taken from Article 92 of the 1982 All People's Defence law, and it's very straightforward. It consists of safe-guarding the independence, sovereignty, territorial integrity, and the social order as defined by the SFRY constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And next I see you deal with the 1983 manual on the strategy of armed conflicts.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And here you emphasize that the role is in protecting the interests of all nations and all nationalities in the SFRY; is that right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. And I think I discuss at other locations in the report the famous slogan "bratstvo i jedinstvo," brotherhood and unity.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. As at page 25 you deal with the issue of command and control, the concept of command and control, and you include a definition from the military lexicon of what command is and -- but I believe here it's indicated that it encompasses also -- I think this is on the next page, on page 26 at the top of that page, I believe we see here that -- it says that: "Command and control encompasses a continuous gathering of information, monitoring of the situation, making decisions, and issuing directives, commands, and orders." And in your experience and from the documents that you have reviewed, how does a commander ensure this continuous gathering of information?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: I just would first like to highlight, I mean, the military lexicon is obviously not the most authoritative document to define command and control. You will find in my reports both definitions from the legislation as well as from a doctrine which all come back to the same elements, but I include the lexicon just for -- to be as complete as possible. The commander organises command and control by basically having a staff, whereby the staff acts as an advisory body and also by organising a reporting system whereby subordinate units continuously report on their activities, I mean their activities that are based on the orders they have received from the commander. And the commander at the same time receives orders from his superiors and all that together is considered in order to -- I mean, it's like a cycle to develop orders for subordinates and also reports, of course, to the superior about the degree of implementation, reports -- the degree of implementation of the orders that have been received from that superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. I may be jumping a few pages here because at page 59 of your report you do deal with the issue of situational awareness; is that right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Indeed. I'm not sure whether the concept of situational awareness as such is defined -- I don't remember it being defined as such in an SFRY armed forces regulation, but the reporting system that is explained and, for example, the obligation for commander to know -- to be familiar with the situation -- I mean, the status position and capabilities of his units two levels down is exactly the same as what in some other armies is called situational awareness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Can you tell us what is this concept of the status and position -- you said two levels down, what does that refer to?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: I will do so by giving an example, Your Honours. If -- I mean, a brigade consists of battalions. Each battalion consists of -- battalion consists of companies, each company consists of platoons, and platoons consists of sections. If the brigade commander wants to give an order -- I mean, he has received -- the brigade commander has received an order from his superior, the division commander, to conduct an attack somewhere, and the brigade commander, I mean, usually has three battalions for that, he will have to decide which battalion will do what where. In order to be able to decide about that he needs to know the status of these battalions. Well, the status of these battalions is determined by the status of the companies of these battalions because the battalion is just a framework of three companies. So for the brigade commander to give -- to use his battalions in the best possible way, he will have to understand the status of the companies of those battalions, this is from two levels down, from brigade, the next level would be battalion, battalions are actually the companies, I mean, it's the companies who do the work, so that's -- that goes back to the second level then is then company level.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Perhaps I may be going into too much detail here, but you just told us the company really does the work. What are you -- can you explain to us what that means?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yeah, maybe it's not -- it's not the most correct English, but I want -- what I tried to say, the means of the battalion, the manpower and the equipment is in the companies, and from -- I mean, and if you go from the company, a company will consist -- when I look back at my experience in an armoured battalion, a tank battalion would consist of three -- we wouldn't call them companies, we called them squadrons, but three squadrons. If a battalion commander received an order from the brigade commander to conduct an attack somewhere, well the attack would be physically conducted by the squadrons, the battalion is just the encompassing level with the staff. There will be of course in addition to the three what I would call combat or tank companies or squadrons, there would be a support company that would also have to provide some kind of support, refuelling, ammunition supply, and so on. But basically the work is done, the mission is implemented by the companies.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: And if you have a company with only -- I mean a weakened company, it cannot have -- it doesn't have the same capacities or capabilities as a stronger company.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. We see as of page 28 you deal with the various government organs such as the Presidency, the Federal Secretariat for National Defence, et cetera, and I'd like you -- I'd like to take you to page 33 where you deal with the Supreme Command. And this is at the bottom of page 33 you refer to the 1983 strategy of armed conflicts. And here it is quoted that: "In war the Presidency of the SFRY performs the functions of the organ of Supreme Command and control over the armed forces of the SFRY." Could you tell us in practice what does that imply with respect to the role of the president during war time, the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: It means that the Presidency, I mean the SFRY Presidency, acts as the highest political authority which issues directives or instructions or orders, I mean depending of the level, to the, as it was in SFRY, the staff of the Supreme Command, which is the -- led by -- which was led by the SSNO, the federal secretary for people's defence. And he and the Supreme Command Staff will then translate these political directives and instructions into military orders for the subordinate units.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. You explained to us a little earlier that the presidents of the six constituent republics were heading -- were the heads of the -- well, the TOs reported to the presidents of the republics. Did the presidents of the republics have any --

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Objection, that misstates what the witness said about that relationship.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Fine, let me rephrase that then. Let me just go back to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Perhaps you could start by telling us what was the role of the president of the republic with respect to the TO?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Again, as I mentioned earlier, we would have to go back to the specific documents because the -- there has been some dispute -- I mean, what I remember from interviewing witnesses -- not witnesses but -- yeah, witnesses, when I was working for the OTP, about the Law on Defence of the Republic of Serbia that was adopted in July 1991, but the TO, I mean, it reports to the president in the context of -- in the area of manning, organisation -- I mean the commander of a TO reports to the president of the republic in relation to manning, organising, planning combat-readiness, and these issues. But during operations involving JNA and TO, as a general rule, the TO would operate under the command of the JNA. And again, if you look at specific cases and especially the situation in fall 1991 in Croatia, we need to look at the specific documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes. We will do that in a moment. Just with respect to what we were dealing with here the Supreme Command, are the presidents of the republics members of the Supreme Command?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yes, they are, as it is foreseen in the regulations. It needs to be mentioned that the Supreme Command, as such, is not mentioned in the 1974 Constitution because at that time President Tito didn't need such a body. It's only later that we see that the term "Supreme Command" is introduced like in the 1983 doctrinal regulation and as well as during the conflict we see that in media and also in other documents the expression "Supreme Command" is being used.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. Now, as of page 39 we see a section here on the Territorial Defence. I would like to turn your attention to that, please. You just explained to us the system with the republics, and I believe it is at page -- sorry -- yes, it is at page 43 where you quote General Kadijevic's memoirs --

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: --- with respect to the role of the TO. Could you tell us a little bit maybe in a nutshell in the late 1980s what transformations, if any, occurs within the system of the relationship between the JNA and the TO?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honour, several things are being done. I'm not sure anymore where it is in this version -- oh, yeah, no, it's on page 49. I mention the Jedinstvo plan which is adopted in 1986, changes the name of the chief of General Staff of the JNA to Chief of General Staff of the SFRY armed forces. So the Chief of General Staff is not only responsible anymore for the JNA but also for the TO. We also see, and that is discussed further in the report, a change in boundaries of certain units, and we see the introduction of the military districts. And then in May 1990 the Presidency adopts a decision to subordinate the weapons -- or for the -- actually, it's for the safekeeping of the weapons of the TO, that is discussed on page 42, to have these TO weapons kept or stored in warehouses under JNA supervision. And Kadijevic and also others see this as measures to increase federal control over republican TOs.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, you make a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Demirdjian --

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Could I please intervene for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: At page 24, line 10, you asked the witness: "Yes, we will do that in a moment. Just with respect to what we were dealing with here about the Supreme Command, are the presidents of the republics members of the Supreme Command?" And perhaps I missed something, but I didn't see the concept of Supreme Command coming up before this question. So now I'm not certain about which Supreme Command we are talking.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, I apologise, Your Honours. I think it was as at page 33 that we had the concept of Supreme Command, I think we had it for a little while on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: But perhaps Mr. Theunens can explain to us how the concept came about. I think you gave us a small explanation earlier, but maybe if we can return to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Is there a problem with the display or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: There is a problem with the B/C/S documents, Mr. Demirdjian. So if you could when you call a document give the B/C/S reference to the Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. With respect for individual documents, I do have the B/C/S version. For the report itself I'm afraid I haven't noted those down, so I will try to see how we can follow the best possible way.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: So here we have the concept of Supreme Command on the screen. Could you explain that to us, Mr. Theunens.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: I just want to highlight the diagram. I didn't take from any regulation. I just put that together myself based on documents I had reviewed. But basically a number of regulations from the 1980s mention the Supreme Command and its command and control role during one of the three states, and these states are the state of war, the state of imminent threat of war, and I think the state of emergency --

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, may I just interrupt you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Could we perhaps zoom in on the English version on the diagram because I don't think it is quite visible. Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So the Supreme Command is basically -- is the Presidency, the highest civilian or political authority, is established during -- or becomes active during one of the three states I just mentioned. And the Supreme Command as the highest command and control body issues instructions or directives or orders to the Supreme Command Staff. The Supreme Command Staff consists of the Federal Secretariat of people's defence which you could more or less compare with the Ministry of Defence with the only difference that in most countries the Ministry of Defence is civilian but in the SFRY the secretary or the federal secretary for people's defence was a colonel-general, at that time Veljko Kadijevic, so he's assisted by his secretariat as well as by the General Staff and the Chief of General Staff. So -- and the orders, at least those I have seen during the preparation of this report and the other reports, military orders most often go from the SSNO to the next command level which would be the military district, whereas the Chief of General Staff, he may also issue some orders but only -- he only does that when he's forwarding similar -- actually, the same instructions he had already received from the SSNO. So there is much less role played by the Chief of General Staff than may be in some other militaries in other countries. In the context of the events we're looking at, it's also important to notice that during fall 1991 and especially spring 1992, the federal secretary for people's defence, Colonel-General Kadijevic, is often absent for health reasons, and then General Blagoje Adzic who is the Chief of General Staff becomes the acting SSNO.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt, and I didn't want to interrupt the witness, but we've lost the realtime transcript, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: It's working on the middle monitors but not on the e-court -- I mean on e-trans; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: It seems to have come back at least on some monitors, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: On e-trans on our computers it's not moving anymore. It's only working on the monitors in the middle screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gosnell, are you okay now?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: It seems to be back. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. So we can continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. Theunens, for that. With -- yes, what I wanted to ask you was this Supreme Command, was it active at all times?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. Based on the documents I reviewed -- I mean, according to the doctrinal documents, it became active when one of the three states was declared, state of war, imminent threat of war, or emergency, but again looking at the events in 1991, even already in spring 1991, media are talking about the Supreme Command, whereas none of these three states had already been declared.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. And when you say that media -- sorry, I'm lost -- losing my LiveNote as well. When you say media were talking about the Supreme Command, in what terms were they referring to the Supreme Command?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: I mean to my recollection they're talking about decisions taken by the Supreme Command or meetings of the Supreme Command or -- yeah, decisions and guidance to the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I think there's a question from the Judges. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Demirdjian. [Interpretation] Witness, generally speaking nowadays when we talk about Supreme Command we mean the head of state or heads of state, as you said, the highest political level, as you said. In this little table that I see on the screen before me there is mention of the federal Presidency of the SFRY, and it is said that the Supreme Command consists of eight members - I'm translating as I speak - one from each of the six republics, and one from each of the two autonomous provinces. Can you tell me, who are the members delegated by republics? Is it, again, the highest political authority, as is the case of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, or would it be any random delegate sent to that body?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, there is a distinction or there is a difference between the president of each of the republics, I mean Slovenia, Croatia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, Serbia, Montenegro, Macedonia on one hand; and then the delegates of these republics in the Presidency. Like, for example -- I haven't mentioned the two provinces, Kosovo and Vojvodina. So each of these republics and provinces has its own president, but that person is not a member of the Presidency. They have each of these republics and provinces has a delegate or has a representative in the Presidency. For example, as you will see later in the report, during the times that are relevant for us, Mr. Borisav Jovic is the representative of the Republic of Serbia in the Presidency, the SFRY Presidency; whereas, Mr. Slobodan Milosevic is the president of the Republic of Serbia. And it's two individual persons with their own responsibilities. And I've tried to highlight that also on page 35, that is, that the president of the republic plays no de jure - when I say "de jure," I mean in accordance with the 1974 Constitution and other legislation -- relevant legislation - so the president of the republic has no command and control role in relation to the armed forces; whereas, the representative of that republic does have such a role. Now, how they interact with each other, that's obviously another matter, but it's a distinction that needs to be made. I hope I clarified the matter, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you very much. It's very clear now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Demirdjian.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, I would like to take you back now to the issue that we were discussing with respect to the TO which we have at page 39 onwards. And again -- first of all, before I ask you any questions about the book that is published by General Kadijevic, could you tell us what are your views with respect to the content in his memoirs?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, his memoirs -- I mean, I focused mainly on his -- the views he expressed on the Supreme Command, his relations with the Supreme Command, as well as his analysis of the operations conducted by the SFRY armed forces and in there he focuses on the JNA, looked in the context of -- seen in the context of other contemporaneous documentation, like official decisions, political and military, I consider him a reliable source and the information he provides on these issues of -- of a high degree of credibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. Now, at page 43 of your report in English, I will try to see if I can find the page number in B/C/S, although it might be a little bit -- oh, yes. I'm sorry, it's page 54, thank you, of the B/C/S version. We see here General Kadijevic describing the decision to disarm the TO and to place it under the control of the JNA, and you quote here, "as 'one of the most important steps taken to paralyze the baneful constitutional concept of the Armed Forces.'" Now, in what context does this come about?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, this corresponds with what I mentioned earlier, that is that in especially in the latter half of the 1980s, senior JNA officers as well as the authority -- I mean, the political authorities in Serbia or -- and others who consider themselves pro-Yugoslav, they consider that republics like Croatia and Slovenia are striving for independence and as -- and in order to implement this desire for greater independence or even total independence and secession from SFRY are transforming their Territorial Defences into armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: You mentioned a little bit earlier that - and this was at page 42 of your report - that there is an order from General -- Colonel-General Blagoje Adzic with respect to the safekeeping of the ammunitions and the weapons of the TO. Might I ask that we display on the screen 65 ter 40, 4-0, which is at tab 29. Yes. Now, I believe we can see the date, it is the 14th of May, 1990; is that right? Do you see this on your screen?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: I do, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. And under item 1 Adzic orders the military district, the air force, and naval district commands together with the TO staffs to organise the take-over, storage, and safekeeping of the complete stock of the TO weapons and ammunition in the JNA supply dumps and depots. Now, first of all, is this the document that you are referring to at page 42 of your report?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And to your knowledge, what impact did this order have at the time?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I haven't been able to make a complete review of the degree of implementation of that order. We had -- we have some documents indicating that, for example, in some parts of the Republic of Croatia indeed weapons of the TO are transferred from storage sites that were under exclusive TO control to storage sites that are under JNA control, but I've also seen reports that actually this order was not fully implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. Perhaps if we could look at 65 ter 41, 65 ter 41, which is at tab 30. The previous document we saw from Blagoje Adzic was dated the 14th of May, 1990. Now we have a document from a week later, the 21st of May, 1990. Are you familiar with this document, Mr. Theunens?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. This is an example of a TO unit in Croatia in -- more specifically in the city of Split, indicating that their weapons have been transferred to another warehouse -- a warehouse under JNA control, a JNA depot.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And does this have any relation with the document we just saw before this one?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Even if -- it refers to a document of the 16th of May, 1990, as opposed to the 14th of May, but it's reasonable to assume that the document of the 16th of May would have referred to the order of General Adzic because Adzic would not issue orders to each and every municipal TO staff. It would most likely have gone through the republican and then the zonal TO staffs.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: These two documents, Your Honours, are in the report. In fact, whenever I don't mention anything, we can assume that the document is in the report. When it's a new document, I'll mention it. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: We talked about the mission of the JNA, and I will -- we'll deal a little bit later this morning with what happened in 1991. For now I'd like us to move to the structure of the SFRY armed forces which you deal with as at page 59 of your report. And I'm very helpfully told that in B/C/S that's page 74, 74/75. Now, you deal here with -- yes, the structure of the territorial organisation of the SFRY armed forces. And if we move on to two pages forward at page 61 we see here that you deal with the branches of the JNA. We have the army, the ground forces, the air force, the air defence. And on the next page, 62, you have the navy. I'd like you to explain to the Trial Chamber the concept of armies. I believe you indicate at page 63 that the armies are abolished and as a peace time military territorial structure was replaced by the term "military district." What are armies and how do they compare to military districts?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Armies in the sense of a hierarchical or structural level of the armed forces -- I mean, the definition you can find on page 62. It's a group of ground forces, all JNA, whereas the military districts, they are part of the state -- I mean, this is explained on page 63. They also -- I mean, they have different boundaries and they could also -- they would also include, I mean at least on a functional level when they conduct exercises and so on, they would also include TO. And the important issue there is that the boundaries of the military districts do not correspond to the boundaries of the republics.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. So are you telling us that the armies did correspond?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: To be honest at this moment I'm not sure. I would have to review that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. Maybe we can return that to a little bit later. So you're telling us that the military districts as of 1988 do not correspond to the boundaries of the republics. With respect to the present case, which military district was the most relevant to the events?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: That would be the 1st Military District, Your Honours, because that covered the eastern part of Croatia as well as northern Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And in -- we'll get back to that in more detail later, but very briefly could you tell who is the chief of the 1st Military District in 1991?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: At the time of the events in 1991, Colonel-General Zivota Panic was the commander of the 1st Military District.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. In the next -- at the next page which is page 64 in English, you explain here that -- or the old concept of armies meant that there were seven armies, one for each republic.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: The new concept of military district changes this dramatically. This is what you just told us. Is there an explanation as to why this change came about?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: I haven't seen documents at the time or official documents where the -- the reasons for these measures because I think the introduction of the military districts has to be seen in the context also of the Adzic order which was based on an instruction from the SFRY Presidency to put TO weapons under JNA control, and then we had the earlier decision to change the Chief of General Staff of the JNA -- I mean, to change the functioning to Chief General Staff of the SFRY armed forces, are all part of measures to increase federal control over the TOs in light of these aspirations among some republics, most obviously Croatia and Slovenia, to -- for more independence or even to secede from the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. Now, without getting into too much detail, could you tell us within military districts what kind of units can one find at the beginning of the conflict, let's say in early 1991?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: I mean, for ground forces you would have corps, divisions, brigades, and so on up to the platoon level. There are also TO units and then -- I mean, since we're talking about the conflict - and I presume that's the reason for your question - we would also see the establishment of temporary units for the conduct of specific operations in specific areas, and those being operational groups, tactical groups, and in some areas assault detachments and assault groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Well, at page 69, actually, you do deal with the concept of operational group.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Could you perhaps give us an explanation of the structure and the role of an operational group?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Summarising what is mentioned in the report, Your Honours, these OGs, TGs, JODs are temporary formations that are established to conduct a specific operation in a specific area, and they are established because they will be forces of different parent units or of a different nature involved. We see from the operational groups and tactical groups that are established in fall 1991 in Croatia by the JNA that they consist of JNA units which may come from different corps. Krajina Serb MUPs, or police, I mean this is mainly in Banja or Lika or Kordun, but in Eastern Slavonia we see JNA units, local Serb TO, TO Serbia, units identified as volunteer detachments. There's even sometimes the use of expressions Chetnik detachment. And all these different forces, they will have to operate together. Now, given the three principles of command and control which are explained earlier in the report, and those are single command and control, unity of command and control, and obligation to implement decisions, the easiest way to implement these or enforce these principles is by creating a new structure with one single commander, the OG or the TG commander, and then all these different units are part of that temporary structure.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Could you tell the Court if this temporary -- the temporary nature of an operational group -- well, what impact does it have on issues such as command and control which we have seen earlier?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, since we are talking about militaries, I would say everything happens on command, i.e., there is an order to establish the OG or the TG or the other temporary formation and there will be an order to disband them. And during the time of existence of the OG and the TG, all forces that are part of the OG and the TG are under the command of the OG and TG commander, unless of course specified differently.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. And with respect to the -- again, the temporary nature of an operational group, in which way is it created and in which way does its existence end?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: It would be done through an order and most often a written order. I mean, it could be done through oral orders, but then one would find a trace of that oral order in a war diary or a situation report. I mean, there should be some kind of a written trace of the decision to establish or abolish it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. And just before we take the break, at page 73 you deal with another organ which is the security administration and the security organs. This is page 73 in the English version and in B/C/S that's page 92. Now, here first we see a quote from the Law on National Defence and let me just see -- yes, I believe you refer to -- just a second, please. Well, before I get to that, could you tell us briefly what is the role and function of the security administration?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Well, they are responsible for security, and that involves also counter-intelligence as well as -- and again, it's explained in the report just to save time, that also involves, for example, investigation of serious crimes against the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: In terms -- with respect to the structure of the armed forces, where does the security administration fit?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: The -- Your Honours, the chief of the security administration or the "uprava bezbednosti," I apologise for my incorrect Serbian declination, is located at the level of the -- it is part of the federal secretariat of people's defence, or the SSNO, and then there will be security organs OB in the different commands, corps command, brigade command, division command. There may also be separate counter-intelligence groups, KOG, established. The security organs will consist of an assistant commander for security who is an advisor to the operational commander, and he may have -- he will have certain assistants. And the interesting -- I mean, relevant maybe to mention here is that the assistant commander for security or the security organ in a unit will be subordinated from an operational point of view to the operational commander, but from a functional point of view he will get instructions from the security administration, for example, as to how to do things. And there are also examples throughout at least 1991 but also earlier with the security administration giving tasks concerning investigations or something directly to security organs located at an operational command level in a brigade, for example, without informing the brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, you explained to us that the security administration, or if we refer to it by its abbreviation the UB, is at the level of the federal secretariat of people's defence, and then you mentioned the security organs, the OB, and then you just mentioned that, you know, for example, we would find them in brigades. Could you tell the Court in which organisational units would you expect to find an OB unit or a security organ basically?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: For sure in brigades, Your Honour, and higher level, of course, corps and divisions. I don't recall having seen reference to security organs at battalion level.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. And, yes, one last question before the break. I think at page 75 under item (c) you say here that the security organs also provide specialist management to the military police. Can you tell us what is that relationship between the security organs and the military police?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. Yes, yes, Your Honours. Again, from an operational point of view, the military police is under the command of the operational commander, but given their specialist tasks, whereby it is explained in the report military police can also conduct investigations in crimes, for those kind of activities the security organs cannot only advise the commander on how to use the military police but can also advise military police commanders on how to do -- how to conduct these activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Theunens.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I believe it is the appropriate time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Demirdjian. Just for the record in -- at page 38, line 20, the word "obey" after security organs should be replaced by OB.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Theunens, we take the first break. We will come back to -- at 11.00. The court usher will escort you out of the courtroom. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please be seated. Yes, Mr. Demirdjian, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Welcome back, Mr. Theunens. I'd like to take you to page 76 of your report, and in B/C/S that is page 95, where you deal with the armed forces of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I will not delve into too much detail. I believe your section is self-explanatory, but suffice it to say there is a TO, a Territorial Defence, in the Republic of Serbia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honours. Maybe very briefly in the report I explain in the following pages what I mentioned earlier that there was some controversy about these -- this defence law which was adopted in July 1991 because it also refers to the president of the republic acting as the commander of the armed forces of the republic, which was not consistent with the SFRY armed forces doctrine in relation to the TO.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And perhaps just to remind us, how does it compare to the SFRY armed forces doctrine, this decision?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: I mean, as we discussed earlier, the commander of the TO is answerable to the president of the republic for a number of issues which I would call managerial issues, i.e., planning, organising, equipping, training, and so on. But in this defence law we see that the president of the republic commands the armed forces. And then further on -- I mean, I'm also referring, sorry, to the 1990 Constitution of the Republic of Serbia, but again you can find all that in this section of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: That's page 78 if we can flip for that. Actually it's the next page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And that actually there is a reference in one of these articles that as long as there are no armed forces defined, the TO will function as the armed forces of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. Now, quickly moving on to page 83, here you deal with the VJ, the Vojska Jugoslavije, and you explain here that the VJ was the successor to the JNA. And I believe it's at page 92 in the English version, which is page 114 in B/C/S, where you explain that there is a high degree of similarity and coherence between the command and control doctrines in the JNA and the VJ. With respect to the VJ leadership itself, how does the composition of the VJ compare with the composition of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: I mean, there are a few differences. First of all, in the -- when the FRY is established, the concept of Territorial Defence is abolished, so the VJ is the only military force, and then the VJ is obviously commanded by the Chief of General Staff and above that political authority the highest authority for defence matters consists -- is the Supreme Defence Council, which you could compare to the Supreme Command as it existed in the SFRY, whereas of course in this situation in the FRY it consists of the presidents of Serbia, Montenegro, and FRY and is presided by the president of FRY and if I recall well the Chief of General Staff has an advisory role.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. And I'm sorry, I don't think I can find it here, you said that this is -- at page 83 you mentioned that the VJ is a successor of the JNA and you make a reference to the FRY Constitution of 1992.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Can you just help us perhaps pin-point a date as to when the VJ succeeds or is created?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yeah, this is in May 1992, but it takes some time to establish it because as a serious -- I mean, reorganisation to happen as there was still a TO in the Republic of Serbia and a TO in the Republic of Montenegro as well as in Vojvodina and Kosovo and all these have to be integrated or abolished or transformed otherwise in order to create the VJ.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: We will get to the factual context later on, but could you just give us in a nutshell what causes the creation of the VJ?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: It's the dissociation of the SFRY -- not the dissociation, but it's the fact, okay, Slovenia had left already in summer of 1991, Croatia in November of 1991, and then Bosnia-Herzegovina in April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. As I say, we'll look at that in more detail later --

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Sorry, I forgot to mention also Macedonia also I believe in April or May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like us to go to page 98 of your report in B/C/S, that's page 120, where you deal with the military justice system in the SFRY armed forces. First you begin at -- yes. You begin with a section on the military discipline system, which is at page 99, and you make a distinction between infractions and offences, et cetera. And then it is at page 100, B/C/S 123, where you deal with the military justice system.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And the role of the office of the military prosecutor. I want to take you to Article 5 of the Law on The Office of the Military Prosecutor which is at page 102 in your report, which is 125 in the B/C/S version. I'm just waiting for the English version to come up on the screen. Now we can focus on the bottom part of the page. Yeah, Article 5 is right there. You indicate here that at Article 5 there is a duty upon the offices of the military prosecution at the units and bodies of the JNA to inform not only the office of the military prosecution about the implementation of the law and their work but also the superior officers and units and bodies of the JNA. I want you to clarify a little bit the terminology here. What is meant by the offices of the military prosecution at the units and bodies of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, as is explained in the law, there is a structure -- I mean, there's not only a system with procedures and rules, but also a structure to implement those procedures and rules. And I don't think I have a detailed breakdown as to how the military prosecution, the military justice system was organised, but it would be plausible to have military prosecution officers or prosecutor officers at the military district level and -- or at the regional level and these -- they may have sub-officers, and all these, I mean, the sub-officers report to the superior officers, and they will at the end report to the military prosecutor at the General Staff level.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And this duty to inform about the implementation of the law and their work, can you tell us in practice how this would translate in practical terms?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is done by periodical reports. There are some included in the section where I discuss the implementation of the system. Further trials I've seen -- I mean, not specifically for the VJ, but, for example, the VRS that there were monthly updates by the military prosecutor officers at the corps levels.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. If we move away from this for a moment and go to the next page, which is page 103 of your report, that's 126 in the B/C/S version, you deal here with the mandate of the military courts. And here you -- I think you quote -- yes, Article 1 of the Law on the Military Courts. Yes. And you indicate here that military courts, as regular courts, try criminal acts committed by military persons and also by other persons when such criminal acts are related to the national defence and the security of the state ..." Now, this is a law of 1977. To your knowledge, does this also apply with relations to violations of the laws of war?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: The -- I mean, for the military personnel, obviously the answer is clear. For non-military and, for example, volunteers, the answer is difficult to give because I -- there are very few examples. I mean, this is discussed further in the reports -- in report, but there are very few examples at least that I am aware of even if we, for example, requested these kind of reports from the military prosecution office or from the military courts to the authorities of FRY and later Serbia while I was working as a military analyst in the Office of the Prosecutor, but we received very little or no answers.
