So it's difficult for me to say whether, for example, members of volunteer units were prosecuted by military prosecutors and whether justice was pursued in front of military courts or, as we all know, later on when there was a war crimes prosecution office established in Belgrade - but this is like 10 or 15 or 20 years after the events - then these people were brought to justice in front of this special war crimes court. So I mean, to answer in shorter manner for civilians I cannot answer on the basis of the information -- the documents that I reviewed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, you do refer at page 106 of your report to the -- to regulations which were adopted in 1988 with respect to the application of international laws of war. At the bottom of that page -- and, I'm sorry, in B/C/S page 108 -- page 107 is page 132 in B/C/S. Here at the bottom of that page you indicate that as a member of the international community of states, Yugoslavia had accepted the rules of international laws of war, and this -- how would you -- with regards to that, how do you view these regulations, the 1988 regulations?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the 1988 regulations, and they were still valid during the 1991 conflict, are consistent with the various international regulations, including Geneva Conventions, and the content is similar to similar regulations that apply to other armed forces, I mean armed forces of other countries.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. And just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: If we could actually display the instructions, it's 65 ter 27 at tab 23.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: While that's coming up, Mr. Theunens, with respect to what you say here at the bottom of page 106, that Yugoslavia had accepted the rules of international laws of war, were you aware of whether they were members of the Geneva Conventions, where Yugoslavia was a state party?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: My understanding is they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. Now, is this the cover page here that we see of the 1988 regulations?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yes, it is, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. And in the English version could we go to page 23 -- sorry, page 21, and in B/C/S it is also page 21. Yes, do you see item number 37 here, jurisdictions -- jurisdiction for trials?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Mm-hmm, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, it says here that trials of military personnel who violate the laws of war which entail criminal liability fall under the jurisdiction of the Yugoslav military courts, and if a member of a foreign armed force violates the laws of war, he shall be tried by the military court with jurisdiction trials, et cetera. Now, does this in some ways correspond to the articles we've seen earlier with respect to the law on the military courts?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: It does and I think it's also relevant to refer to one of your first questions this morning, that was, that anyone -- I'm paraphrasing, anyone who joins the defence of the country shall be considered a member of the armed forces and is therefore also subject to these regulations.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. Now, in relation to the Law on Armed conflicts you also quote I believe it is Article 93 of the Law on People's Defence. And this is Exhibit L10 which is at tab 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: If we could display this law.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, sorry, it is at page 105 of your report in English and B/C/S I haven't noted it down, but it's probably page 127/128.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Okay, so with respect to the Law on All People's Defence could we go in English to page 60, 6-0. Yeah. Yes, and we can zoom on Article 93, and in B/C/S it is page 16.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And again here we see Article 93 which provides that: "During combat activities, members of the Armed Forces are obliged at all times to abide by the rules of international law of war on the humane treatment of wounded and captured enemies ...," et cetera. Can I ask you, I mean, with respect to documents that you have reviewed, are you able to tell the Court what was the level of training of officers and soldiers of the SFRY armed forces with respect to international humanitarian law?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm -- I don't have -- I haven't seen any training programmes of -- or I don't recall seeing, like, annual training documents or programmes for the JNA or SFRY armed forces. However, the specific orders, for example, from the command of the 1st Military District or Operational Group South for the operations conducted in fall 1991 in the wider Vukovar area, they repeatedly referred to the importance of abiding by the international laws of war and the humane treatment of prisoners and civilians, and in my report I also refer to guide-lines and instructions from General Kadijevic, I mean, so superior commanders, as well as General Adzic in this domain. So I think it's reasonable to conclude from that that the officers and their personnel were aware of the obligations and were also regularly reminded of those.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. On the same page of your report, at page 105 you referred to Chapter 16 of the SFRY Criminal Code which again lists offences against humanitarian law. And perhaps as a general overview, could you tell the Court what was the state of the legislation at the time and how did it compare with the existing legal framework with respect to international humanitarian law?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: I'm not a lawyer and I don't pretend to be one, but my impression is that all these things are consistent and they all come back to the same base line, that is, that what we in the military know as the Geneva Conventions and our obligations in relation to laws of armed conflict and international humanitarian law, that all these aspects are codified also in the SFRY, not only in legislation as what we are quoting in now -- now from, but also in military regulations like the 1988 regulations in that military personnel is familiar with those and are during the combat operations also reminded of those.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. I'd like to move now to another topic which is at page 116 of your report and that's 143 in the B/C/S version, and this is the topic of investigation and prosecutions of violations of the laws and customs of war. Now -- perhaps maybe generally before we move to the specific, could you tell the Court which Army of organs are in charge of investigating such criminal offences?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, two types of organs or structures are responsible for these activities, those are the security organs and the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And I believe you quote here the rules of service of the security organs, the 1984 rules of service, and you have a quote here with respect to their specific task relating to the detection and prevention of serious crimes.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: I do and I just maybe draw your attention to the fact that the article -- the paragraph 7 of the 1984 rules of service of the security organs refers to actually crimes to the armed forces consisting of theft or damage of arms and ammunition and property crime, but we see - and again these documents are discussed in the report that during the 1991 conflict security organs also investigate crimes or alleged -- crimes that could correspond to violations of the laws of war. For example, in the Skabrnja area as well as also in Baranja and eastern Slovenia there are several reports by security organs discussing crimes or serious crimes that would fall under violations of the international laws of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. On the next page, page 117 of your report, you deal with the authority of the security organs to detain a suspect for up to three days.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And you quote an article here of the rules of service, that's Article 45, I believe, and you indicate that the decision on detention which must be justified is issued by the senior officer of the security organ of an army command; is that right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yes, that is what the article states.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. And the next quote you have here is: "When placing a person in detention before the commencement of an investigation, security organs may not question the detained tern as a suspect but are authorised to conduct interviews with him aimed at procuring necessary information." Can you tell us what this refers to?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: In my understanding, Your Honours, this refers to -- I mean, the difference between a criminal investigation where the military police would be involved and most likely members of the military prosecutor's office, I mean the criminal/judicial investigation on one hand, and on the other hand the work of security organs who are -- whose task is to gather information concerning potential security threats to the armed forces. Criminal investigation is not their main task; that is taken care of by other organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. I'd like to take you to the implementation of the military justice system, which starts at page 122 in the English version and that's page 150 in the B/C/S version. Here you start with your conclusion in the first paragraph of the section. Yes, it's up there. And can you briefly summarise for the Trial Chamber what is your conclusion with respect to the implementation of the military justice system?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. Your Honours, the conclusion is that this system is -- appears to be functioning and is for what friendly armed forces -- members of the friendly armed forces is concerned focused on what I would call the typical military crimes, like desertion or crime against the armed forces, whereas otherwise -- I mean, in relation to violations of the international laws of war or related crimes, it's mainly focused on activities of members of the opposing armed force. And again, I don't have so many documents -- I didn't have so many documents available to draw conclusions from, but I do remember that between 2003 and 2007, several requests were sent to the Republic of -- to FRY and to the Republic of Serbia for reports of the work of the military prosecutor offices versus a military court in order for us -- for me at least to achieve an understanding of their activities and in relation to, for example, reports we had seen from security organs concerning alleged violations of the laws of war committed by members of the JNA or members of volunteer or other units operating under JNA command during the 1991 conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. I will skip over the whole factual basis of the operations in Eastern Slavonia. I will come to that later. I would like you to take a look at a document which relates to this issue from the 2nd of December, 1991. This is 65 ter 748 at tab 220. You see the cover page here which says "Bulletin." Just perhaps by way of introduction, I believe there are a few of these bulletins which you have used in your report. Could you tell the Trial Chamber with respect to their content and their preparation, what are your views with respect to the information contained therein?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the bulletin was a document -- sorry, a publication in English issued by the SSNO, so the federal secretariat for people's defence. I believe it was done by the administration for moral guidance. And it was specifically intended for the international community, be it diplomats or embassies as well as the EU observers or even the UN, and it gave -- it reflected the SSNO's views on the conflict. There were reports on the conduct of operations, on alleged crimes committed by the other side, and various issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And if we could go to page 4 in the English version, we can stay on page 1 in the B/C/S version. Yes. In the middle of that page we see a statement by the commander of the 1st Army District. Can you see that, Mr. Theunens?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yes, I see it, Mr. Demirdjian.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And we see here that forensic medicine and criminal investigation team of the JNA is engaged in identifying persons killed in Vukovar. And the next paragraph we see here that criminal proceedings are imminent or have already been opened at military or regular courts against a number of members of the Croatian paramilitary formations suspected of committing these and other crimes. What is your view, again, with respect to this type of information?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, this corroborates what I said earlier, that is, that the investigative and prosecution effort concerning alleged violation of the laws of war are concentrated on members of the opposing armed force and in this case in looking at the conflict in Croatia in 1991, that -- those members are members of the Croatian National Guard and Croatian forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. Now, generally speaking and if we're getting into specifics, can you explain to the Judges what kind of information was available to the Belgrade leadership at the time with respect to crimes committed by Serbian soldiers?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: On one hand, Your Honours, you have reports from security organs and sometimes military police. But of course I have seen these reports. Sometimes I see follow-up documents -- I have seen follow-up documents from a higher level in the military, but I cannot -- I do not know from the documents that were available to me to what extent these documents, for example, from the 1st Military District were then forwarded to, for example, the Supreme Command. That is one type of documents. On the other hand, there is, for example, what I quoted a letter dated 21st of January, 1992, by the US Helsinki Watch Committee, which was sent to the president of Serbia, Mr. Milosevic; the acting federal secretary for people's defence, General Blagoje Adzic, I mean those two. And this is quoted on page 123. And the fact that -- I think that's on the next page, yeah, that a few weeks later, I believe, let's check -- yeah, three weeks later the chief of cabinet of President Milosevic answers to the letter, the Helsinki Watch letter, indicates that indeed they have received it - I mean "they," I mean President Milosevic and his staff - have received it and they have reviewed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: If we could look at this report from Helsinki Watch, it's 65 ter 892 at tab 246. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, we see on the cover page as you've indicated, that this is addressed to the president of the Republic of Serbia, Slobodan Milosevic, as well as General Adzic. Looking just at the first sentence: "The US Helsinki Watch Committee is deeply troubled by reports of serious human rights abuses by the Serbian government and the Yugoslav Army." If we could turn to the second page in both versions, we can see the title there: "Rules of War Violations in the Croatian Conflict." And the third paragraph here states that: "The Serbian government has also condoned and, in some cases, supported the formation of at least three paramilitary groups in Serbia which operate in Croatia." Can you give us a little bit of a background with respect to these paramilitary groups?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: You want me to explain the groups in -- addressed in this document? Because then I would have to see the page, but otherwise I have reviewed actually other documentation, documentation from the Republic of Serbia Ministry of Defence as well as, for example, answers provided by government officials of the Republic of Serbia to questions in the parliament where they are -- indeed, members of the parliament inquire or ask questions about various paramilitary or volunteer groups that are being established. And again, from related documents - and I mean by that official documents - one indeed can conclude that the -- that the then-authorities of the Republic of Serbia, mainly the president, the Ministry of Interior, and the Ministry of Defence, condone or even support the creation of these volunteer groups notwithstanding actually -- and we haven't discussed that but you can find it in the Law of Defence that Article 118 of the July 1991 Law of Defence of the Republic of Serbia states that only the state authorities are competent to plan, organise, equip, and maintain, I believe, armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Now, this is a very lengthy report. I just wanted to look at two more excerpts. If we can go to page 3 in the English version. Yes. Do you see the entry for August 1st in Dalj?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: I do, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And here the Helsinki Watch is reporting that after the JNA occupied Dalj, Serbian paramilitary groups reportedly searched the village for Croatian soldiers, police officers, and civilians and killed many of those who were found wounded. That's one example we have there. And if we could go to page, just a second, 7. Yes, under the title: "November 18 - Vukovar," there is a general assessment first of the situation in Vukovar. And then we see the last sentence in that paragraph that: "On the basis of interviews with displaced persons from Vukovar and foreign journalists ... Helsinki Watch has reason to believe that many Croatian men, both civilians and combatants who had laid down their arms, were summarily executed by Serbian forces after Vukovar's fall." I'm not going to go through every example we have here, but you told us that there was a response from Milosevic's chief of cabinet; is that right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And in the documentation that you have reviewed, have you seen with respect to the Serbian authorities anything else with respect to the crimes that are listed here?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: When I -- when we look at the answer that is sent by the chief of cabinet of Mr. Milosevic, i.e., Goran Milinovic, he, for example, states in paragraph 2 that the president of the Republic of Serbia asked competent organs of the republic to investigate the crimes, and even if citizens of the Republic of Serbia participated in those crimes they will be brought to justice. Again, based on the documentation I had available to me, I have no -- not seen any indications of that. I think this is discussed further on in the report and maybe in the Seselj section, but, for example, in relation to volunteers who are affiliated or recruit through the Serbian Radical Party and who has been we discussed the operations in Vukovar operated in the so-called Leva Supoderica TO detachment. It's only -- I think it's in the latter half of 1993 when there is a political fallout between Mr. Milosevic and Mr. Seselj that members of Seselj's volunteers, i.e., individuals recruited through the SRS, Serbian Radical Party, or SS war staff, are arrested and investigated but they are not investigated for war crimes but for the illegal possession of weapons. And again, the few cases I remember they were released quite quickly or maybe sentenced to minor sentences. But there was, as far as I recall, no investigation of their alleged involvement in serious violations or in serious crimes and violations of the laws of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, at the time you explained to us earlier that the security administration and the security organs were in charge of detecting and preventing crimes. Were you aware of any exchange of information between the security organs or the security administration with the state security in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I think there is at least one example included in my report. I would just like to clarify that according to the 1988 regulations any officer who sees or is informed that the crime has occurred or may have occurred is obliged to inform the competent bodies or organs in order to ensure that the adequate measures are taken. I don't recall the exact article number, but I think it's important to highlight it's not just confined to security organs and military police. Anyone who discovers or who believes that a crime may have been committed has to report it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. In that context could I ask you to look at Exhibit D17, which is at tab 291. Yes. Mr. Theunens, this is a document here we see from the state security department. Have you -- are you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: I am, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And if you look at the preamble, what does it say here in respect to the information received from the SSNO?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Well, it shows that the security administration UB at the SSNO on the 26th of May, so one day before this report, shared information with the state security department in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And looking at the information contained herein, what -- what type of events does it relate to?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: The first paragraph talks about -- or discusses the killing of 17 residents in -- of Lovas village on the 18th of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes. And we'll not go through the entire report, but is it your understanding that this is the type of information contained in this five-page report?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yes, and I mean if I recall well that there's various crimes -- I mean, there's the Lovas crime but there may be also other crimes or alleged crimes are discussed. I would have to go through the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, very well --

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: But it shows that there is an exchange of information between the security organs at the SSNO and the state security department.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And this document is dated the 27th of May. Now, could we look at very briefly 65 ter 1131, which is tab 289. I believe this is a document that is also cited in your report. The title here is: "Information." Yes, we see the English version now. Crimes against the civilians committed by members of the paramilitary and the volunteer formations in the Republic of Serbian Krajina. At the bottom we see the date which is the 26th of May. And actually if we scroll -- yes, at the top we see it's from the federal secretariat for the national defence, the SSNO --

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Security administration, so it's the document actually we referred to earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And if we go to page 2, yes, do we -- do you find here in the first paragraph which starts with: "While carrying out the tasks from within their authority ..."

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: The -- how this information was gathered, the information contained in this report?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours, I mean the text is very straightforward. It talks about how security organs while conducting their regular activities collected information concerning alleged crimes or they actually call it serious criminal acts that are described and this is by members -- I mean, committed by members of the -- of volunteer formations who were a part of the TO of the S -- of Eastern Slavonia, western Srem, and Baranja, i.e., the SAO.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes. And that's the part of the sentence which I'd like you to focus on for a minute. It says that crimes committed by members of the volunteer formations who were for the most part on the strength of the TO of Eastern Slavonia --

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: What do you make out of this in respect to the fact that the volunteer formations were part of the TO?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: This comes back to what I said in the beginning, Your Honours, that according to the legislation that anyone who wants to join the armed struggle in defence of the country and who is not a member of the JNA will be considered a member of the TO -- actually, I'm combining now two articles, because the literal text says that any armed formation that is not a part of the JNA will be considered TO, which comes back to the same. And since the law did not foresee the establishment of volunteer units, I make a distinction between units and individuals, while these volunteer formations or units were amalgamated or were considered TO.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, at the bottom of page 2 we see a first instance that is reported here with respect to events in the village of Lovas. And we see here, again at the bottom of that page, that about 40 members of the Valjevo TO detachment participated in the action and approximately ten members - if we can go to the next page, please - yes, ten members of the Dusan Silni detachment under the command of certain Joca who left the unit immediately after the event, are you familiar with this unit, the Dusan Silni detachment?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, it's one of these volunteer formations or paramilitary groups from Serbia who participated in the fighting in this -- here in Eastern Slavonia, Baranja, and western Srem. And just for the sake of completeness, Valjevo TO detachment is a TO detachment originating from the city of Valjevo in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now that you've mentioned that, can you tell us a little bit, what was the extent of the involvement of TO units from Serbia in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Again, I think I want to highlight two aspects. First of all, referring to what we said about military districts, whereby military districts consist of JNA or cover, sorry, cover TO and JNA units, that we see indeed that TO units of the area covered by that military district are participating in the conflict on the side of the JNA. But we also see TO units from other parts of Serbia participating in these operations. And that is not only the case in Eastern Slavonia, Baranja, and western Srem but also other parts of Croatia, but I think in the report there is a document included that refers to several TO units and detachments from the Republic of Croatia, even outside the area covered by the 1st Military District that are participating in the operations in Eastern Slavonia, Baranja, and western Srem.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: First, the document we're looking at now is from May of 1992. I'd like you to look at a document from the month of November 1991 which is 65 ter 6032 at tab 561.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, this is a document that is not in the expert's report.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes. We see here a document of the JNA command of the town of Ilok of the 23rd of November, 1991. Mr. Theunens, have you had the opportunity to review this document?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. This is one of the many documents that were available to me after July 2012, and I understand they were obtained by the -- or the translation was -- and even they were obtained by the OTP after July or around July 2012. So this is a document I reviewed during my second stay here in September/October 2012.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. Now, we see that this document is sent to the command of the 1st PGMD. We'll come in more detail with respect to the units available, but can you tell the Court what is the 1st PGMD?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: PGMD stands -- I mean, it's explained the Proletarian Guards Mechanised Division, whereby proletarian guards means that it's not a regular unit, I mean, proletarian refers also to traditions of the Second World War. We just have to be careful when we see guards that we don't confuse it with the Guards Motorised Brigade which is a totally different unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. Now, at the bottom of this page under item 7 we see -- and if we can scroll down a little bit on the -- on page 1 of the English version. Yes, thank you. We see here that intensive normative work is being done on establishing local commands and ensuring their functioning. The next sentence reads: "In the course of the day paramilitary organisations from," if we can move to the next page, "the Dusan Silni detachment were chased out of the village of Lovas and parts of the local TO were placed under a single command of TO commands present in that area." Now, do you have information as to the reasons behind this chasing out of the Dusan Silni detachment?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: I mean, the document here doesn't say why they were chased out, but there is a report by the -- I think it's a weekly or biweekly report by the Lieutenant-Colonel Eremija and it's cited in my report toward the assistant commander for morale guidance of the 1st PGMD, where he refers to -- I mean serious crimes in the village of Lovas, and if I am -- if my recollection is right, he identifies Dusan Silni as one of the groups that is responsible for those crimes. So it may well be that one is related to the other, but there is obviously a time gap between the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And you mention that Milan Eremija is the assistant commander of the 1st PGMD?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: For morale guidance. I mean, there are several assistant commanders and he's for morale guidance.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. And here we see that the document is signed by Colonel Milan Belic. Are you familiar with this name?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yes, I've seen him before. I mean, he's the -- he's identified as town commander in the town of Ilok, and it could be that he -- I mean, that he is then assistant commander for civil affairs of the 1st Proletarian Guards Mechanised Division, I believe he is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. Now, before we look at the Eremija report, might I ask Your Honours to tender this document which is 65 ter 6032.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Shall be assigned Exhibit P1683. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Let's go then to Exhibit P78.50 which is at tab 135. Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, you've discussed this document in your report and we see here that it's from the command of the 1st PGMD on the 23rd of October, 1991. Now, the document we just saw earlier from Milan Belic was from the 23rd of November, so this is a month earlier, and it is sent to the command of the 1st Military District. Just for the Trial Chamber's understanding, what is the relationship between the 1st PGMD and the 1st Military District?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, at that time the 1st PGMD is one of the subordinate units of the 1st Military District and it's operating in the southern part of Eastern Slavonia, in Western Srem.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: If we can go to page 2 in the English version, it's item number 4, I believe it is also page 2 in the B/C/S version. And if we can scroll down to the bottom of page 2 in the English version, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: The third bullet point at the bottom of that page indicates that: "In the combat activities of the 1st PGMD, the main motive behind the presence of several groups of different paramilitary formations from Serbia, Chetniks, the Dusan Silni Detachment, and various self-styled volunteers, it is not to combat the enemy but to loot the people's property and engage in the sadistic abuse of innocent civilians of Croatian nationality." And if we go to the next page in the English version we can remain on that same page in the B/C/S version. You see the first paragraph which deals with the activities of the Dusan Silni Detachment, where they had 80 Croatian citizens were physically abused and four of the Lovas villagers were killed. And the next paragraph deals with the minefield -- civilians were used for clearing the minefield. With respect to this event, the clearing of minefield, have you seen other documents which refer to this event?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: You mean in the context of Lovas?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, we just saw the earlier exchange of information between the security administration UB at the SSNO and the state security. And I believe in 2012 there was a trial in Serbia for the war crimes prosecutor for these events for -- sorry, 2011 --

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: -- for these events, so -- and I would just add -- I mean, Eremija is entitled to write about these things because he's responsible for moral guidance, I mean for morale of the troops, and he considers that these activities have a negative impact on morale, so his role is not to investigate crimes but his role is to highlight factors that impact -- in this case have a negative impact on the morale of the troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, he is an assistant to the commander of the 1st PGMD; is that right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: That is correct, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And what other units would you expect to find an assistant commander for morale and guidance, which levels perhaps?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: I mean, for sure starting at the brigade level and then upwards, and I -- I'm not sure anymore at the battalion level whether -- I mean, according to JNA doctrine, a battalion doesn't have a command but there is still a commander and there are a number of staff officers and for sure someone will take care of morale guidance but it could be that it's accumulated with another function.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: But given the doctrine, moral guidance was one of the key -- is an important aspect in the JNA -- I mean the doctrine of unity, brotherhood and unity, moral guidance is an important aspect in the training and education of soldiers and their behaviour during combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. Now, the previous document which was admitted as P1683, the one from Milan Belic, is on the 23rd of November. At that time what was the state of combat operations at the end of November?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: I mean, now we are jumping a bit, but a cease-fire agreement -- I mean, many of -- an agreement was -- I think it was for a cease-fire, but there was an agreement reached in Geneva on the 23rd of November. I mean, the main factor at that stage was the fall of Vukovar theoretically on the 18th but basically on the 20th of November. And then on the 23rd the warring parties and I think Mr. Vance or another international mediator met in Geneva and they agreed I think on a comprehensive cease-fire, and this is then consolidated in early January for a further cease-fire. So basically there is a cease-fire. The JNA is still in the area of Eastern Slavonia, Baranja, and western Srem, and is gradually preparing for handing over authority to the local SAO SBWS authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And with the end of the combat activities there, what is then the status of units such as the Dusan Silni Detachment, some volunteer or paramilitary formations, what happens to them?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: We would have to look at the specific documents because, I mean, from the various documents I've seen they are still in the area. They're not fighting but they're still doing -- conducting certain activities. Some documents mention that they are involved in crimes. Some groups are exploiting natural resources. When I say "crimes," it involves petty crime but also harassment of minorities and so on. But I think it's the most useful would be to look at the specific documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes. Now, if I can return to the -- to your report where you were still discussing the issue of the implementation of military justice, I believe at one -- at page 125 which in the B/C/S version is 153 you refer to a report prepared by the office of the military prosecutor of the VJ in November of 1992. And you quoted here -- and just for the record that document is in the report and it's 65 ter 1378 - you quote here that criminal proceedings were initiated against 125 members of the Croatian armed forces and against one member of the JNA. So what is your conclusion based on these figures?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: The conclusion based on these figures, Your Honours, and also when looking at this particular document in the context of the other documents, because that is what analysis is about, it leads to conclusion that the military justice system is implemented in a selective manner, that is, that investigations for -- and prosecution of serious crimes is focused on members of the opposing armed force because I mean there is a major inconsistency between on one hand what security organs and here, for example, what Eremija, I mean, the assistant commander for moral guidance is saying on the one hand, and on the other hand then these kind of summarising statements or reports by the military prosecutors and the military courts.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now it is correct to say that on the next --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: One moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry to interrupt. There's just one correction for the record. The report actually says that it was not against one member of the JNA but against one member of the armed forces of the SFRY. And just given the answers by Mr. Theunens, it's a distinction of some relevance.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, actually. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, on the next page, Mr. Theunens, it is correct that you're covering the report, the annual report, in 1993, which was prepared by the military prosecutor's office, I believe; is that right -- or the military court, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And here you've pretty much extracted, if I'm correct, the percentages of crimes that had been investigated?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: That is correct. And, I mean, I didn't have many documents. I just had these annual documents but they're still quite indicative.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And you had also similar reports for the following years; is that right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Exactly. We cover 1993, 1994, and 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. Now, we see here the numbers. Most of the crimes that are processed appear to be crimes against the VJ, right, 66.9 per cent?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. And then we see property crimes at 18 per cent.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Crimes against traffic safety and crimes against misconduct for personal gain. Now, how does this -- how does this connect with the conclusions you made at the beginning of the -- of this section of your report?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Well, it -- I think it would corroborate the conclusions because, again, I included 1993 to 1995 because 1992 -- I mean, in simple terms nothing happened. We see that in 1992 the effort for prosecution -- for investigation and prosecution is focused on members of the opposing armed forces. So then I tried to find out whether during the later years, I mean subsequently, there was any effort to investigate the crimes that had been reported, for example, by security organs and others, crimes committed by or allegedly committed by members of volunteer units and/or members of the JNA in 1991, but the conclusions are the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. I'd like to move to another section of your report --

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't know if it's the appropriate time to take a break, I'm moving to -- no, five more minutes I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, okay. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: As of page 133 of your report you deal with the SFRY armed forces and the conflict in Croatia, and here 133 is 163 in the B/C/S version. And the title we have here is: "The Evolution Within the SFRY Armed Forces Supreme Command." And you deal on this page, at the bottom of the page, and this is something you mentioned earlier, I believe, the activation of the Supreme Command; is that right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. Could you explain to us for -- with respect to the diagram we see on the screen, what is it exactly that we're looking at?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is a diagram I drew myself. It's not based on a specific document, but I drew myself on the basis of reviewing several documents and it shows what I highlighted earlier, that is, that -- okay, even if it doesn't show the Supreme Command as such but the federal Presidency of the SFRY is the Supreme Command. It is assisted by the SSNO, who is the chief of staff of the Supreme Command Staff, and he will have with him his deputy, Chief of General Staff, then the sector commanders -- I mean the assistants to the SSNO, as well as the chief of cabinet and the head of the security administration. And he uses -- I mean, those people advise him and then he -- the SSNO prepares military directives and instructions and orders for the military districts who are doing the actual -- conducting the actual operations. So we have three army districts consisting of ground forces, the 1st, the 3rd, and the 5th. There is a naval military district which actually consisted of naval elements but also the 9th Corps. And then there is the air force and the air defence. And then maybe the -- on the right side is a small typo. It shouldn't be the 1st Motorised Guards Brigade. It should be the 1st Guards Motorised Brigade, GMTbr, and actually you can also drop the 1, and they are through the chief of cabinet of the SSNO directly subordinated to the SSNO.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Could you explain to us, and maybe we could zoom in to that right part of the diagram, please. Could you explain to us how it is that there is a brigade located there at that level under the chief of cabinet of the SSNO?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Guards Motorised Brigade is an elite unit and its task is -- include the protection of the Supreme Command, I mean of the -- the Presidency and in times of -- I mean, one of the three states, the Supreme Command, it is also a unit that is used as a ceremonial guard and they guarded a number of official buildings and monuments in Belgrade. I think of importance is also as we will see in Vukovar that the Guards Motorised Brigade had two military police battalions as compared to one for regular brigades. And in these military police battalions or in its regular battalions, it had also anti-terrorist units which no other unit had. So the Guards Motorised Brigade, even if they had a ceremonial duty, I mean you would see them conducting or present at ceremonies, they were responsible for protecting the Presidency, and in one of the three states, the Supreme Command, and they could also conduct hostage release and similar operations which -- it's an elite unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: In very broad terms, Mr. Theunens, I'm sure we don't have specific numbers, but could you tell us what was would be the strength of a battalion?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: I -- I mean, I prefer not to say anything because during the war the strengths continuously change, but it -- regular infantry battalion could be 900 people but it could be much less too. So I don't have -- we never -- I mean, during the Vukovar trial, we -- I don't think we ever learned the theoretical strength of the Guards Motorised Brigade, but it was a strong brigade because I think it had two or three infantry battalions, two military police battalions, it had a tank battalion and then the supporting elements. It was a much stronger brigade than other brigades.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And we see it placed there under the chief of the cabinet of the SSNO?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Next to it we see the head of the security administration, Colonel-General Vasiljevic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. And I mean I guess you will come to that, but on the 30th of September, 1991, the Guards Motorised Brigade is resubordinated from the SSNO to the command of the 1st Military District, i.e., when they are deployed or when they are sent to the Vukovar area.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: To your knowledge, are there other units such as the guards motorised brigades that are -- I don't know if I could say it floating this way or are they usually under one of the military districts?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: I mean, in peace time this is the only unit at that time, I mean 1991 -- I mean in the SFRY, sorry, that was directly subordinated to the SSNO.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. And here we -- the -- in blue at the bottom we saw the military districts.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: These are the organisational units which were called armies before 1988; is that right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yes, and whereby of course the composition and the unit boundaries changed with the transformation of armies into military districts.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Is there any clarification necessary on this, Your Honour s?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Pardon?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Do you require any clarification on this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. I will move to a brand new topic now, so perhaps it would be a good time to stop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. Mr. Theunens, this is the second break. We will come back at 12.45. You will be escorted out of the courtroom. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Demirdjian, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, can we go to page 135 of your report, in the B/C/S version we're looking at page 165 -- actually, 134, sorry. You explain here -- well, let's wait for it to come up. Yes. Thank you. You explain here how in -- around May 1991 Stipe Mesic, the Croatian member of the SFRY Presidency, fails to obtain the required number of votes from the other members of the Presidency. And at the bottom of that paragraph 2, General Kadijevic who is the federal secretary for people's defence does not recognise Mesic as the new supreme commander of the SFRY. So, first of all, can you explain to us a little bit of this concept of a rotating chairmanship of the Presidency, how did that work?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I recall well, every six months the Presidency would rotate among the eight members of the Presidency, and the 15th of May it was the turn of the Croatian member of the SFRY Presidency, Mr. Stipe Mesic to take over, but he didn't obtain the votes and then the events happened as you described.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: What is the background to Kadijevic's position and the fact that Mesic fails to obtain the required number of votes?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: I mean, these are two different aspects of the same issue I would say, and the causes are at least related to each other. At that stage Croatia -- I mean, there is a movement in Croatia -- a strong movement in Croatia for independence and even secession from the SFRY and various statements are made by various people, including Mr. Mesic, and I haven't analysed that in this report. And again referring to the book of Mr. Kadijevic, my view to breakup, he describes in his book that these kind of statements and the general policies pursued by Mr. Mesic and other senior members of the Croatian Democratic Union, HDZ, are incompatible with the status of supreme commander of the SFRY or armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And on that same page you quote also the published diary of Borisav Jovic. Here it says "acting" but I believe we have an errata sheet which specifies that he was the outgoing chairman of the SFRY Presidency; is that right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honours. There was a typo, ellipsis.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, as an outgoing member of the chairmanship, how much of a role does Jovic have?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I mean as a result of the events that are developing at that stage in the SFRY, the SFRY Presidency's functions obviously affected by those events, and we see that even if the EC intervenes to ensure that Mr. Mesic could achieve or take over the post -- take over the post of chairman, it's not really working also because there are even meetings where he doesn't show up. And at that stage, I mean, we're talking between May and the end of the year, the conflict in Croatia is developing and becomes a general conflict in areas that the JNA and then also the leadership of Serbia considers Serb. So the SFRY Presidency is not really functioning anymore as the Supreme Command, and then we see again based on, for example, the memoirs of Borisav Jovic that a kind of a de facto structure becomes active and that de facto structure involves not only Mr. Jovic but also Mr. Milosevic who is the president of the Republic of Serbia at the time; General Kadijevic who is the SSNO; as well as General Adzic who is the Chief of General Staff of the SFRY armed forces. And they have regular meetings and these meetings can also involve Mr. Bulatovic, who is the president of Montenegro at the time and even I think Mr. Branko Kostic, who is the -- becomes the acting chairman and I think he's representative of Vojvodina if I'm not wrong, representative of Vojvodina in -- or of Montenegro in the Presidency, I may be wrong. I would have to check that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: No problem. This paragraph carries on to the next page, and these regular meetings that you were referring to, it appears that at least according to Jovic's book, that during these meetings he, Jovic, and Slobodan Milosevic would occasionally give directions -- or, sorry, instructions to General Kadijevic. Now, what does this -- how does that impact the role of the JNA at the time?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, the starting point is the constitutional role of the JNA, which is, among other things, as we discussed to maintain the territorial integrity of the SFRY. And we see on one hand we have these meetings and the discussions at the meetings and where certain instructions or guidances are given on the one hand, and on the other hand we see the activities of the JNA and the forces under its command on the terrain. We see that that mission -- the constitutional mission gradually changes, whereby at least initially the JNA also tries to act as an interposing force, trying to separate armed -- the two armed sides, if I can express myself that way, i.e., Croatian forces on one hand and Serbian forces on the other hand. And we can explain what we mean by these terms. They try to separate these parties, but in a number of areas basically they consolidate Serbian control over parts of Croatia. And later on we also see that basically the JNA and the forces under its command during the operations they are conducting in Croatia are, in fact, fighting to achieve control over areas that are considered Serb by, for example, Mr. Milosevic, Jovic, and the others who are involved in these what I would call the de facto Supreme Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: On that note, at page 137 of your report - and that's 168 in the B/C/S version - you make a reference to a meeting that took place on the 5th of July, 1991. And again, this is from the diaries of Borisav Jovic. And here you indicate that according to the book a number of demands are expressed in relation to the role of the JNA and Jovic and Milosevic appear to have asked Kadijevic to concentrate the main forces of the JNA in Croatia along specifically -- well, described lines here --

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yeah. Now, could you tell us, first of all, we see an axe Karlovac to Plitvice, and then in Baranja, Osijek-Vinkovci, what is the significance of these axis?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Well, these are basically the western and the eastern limits of what according to Mr. Jovic is the area the JNA should have to cover based on the instructions of Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And in respect of the context of the time that we see this is on the 5th of July, what would have prompted or what did prompt Jovic and Milosevic to express this demand?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: I mean, obviously there are several events happening. We had the conflict in Slovenia and its independence, we have the declaration of independence in Croatia, I think 25th of June, we have had already armed clashes between Serbs and Croats and various parts of Croatia. So I mean, there is a widening of armed clashes in Croatia between Serbs and Croats in areas -- predominantly in areas with a significant Serb presence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. Now, you carry on at the next page at 138, which is page 170 in the B/C/S version, and here you quote Kadijevic who states that the constitutionally defined task of the SFRY armed forces, including the JNA, against an internal -- external and internal aggression is radically changed. Do you see that there at the top of the page?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. And this is -- I mean, the radically is quoted from Kadijevic's book. It's not me who put it there. It's taken from his book as well as the text in italics below, and I think it corresponds with what I just said.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And the first bullet point here says that it radically change into, first, defence of the Serb nation in Croatia and national interests of the Serb nation. At the time and based on the material that you have viewed, how do you view Kadijevic's perception that the Serb nation in Croatia needs to be defended?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: I mean, these kind of issues which we see in many contemporaneous conflicts are always difficult to assess as an outsider, but for anyone who is to some extent familiar with the history of the conflict in the former Yugoslavia, I think people will agree that there is a massive use of propaganda by all sides, whereby the other side is described as a threat, wants to maybe exterminate the other group, and by doing so -- and some -- I will clarify, some actions are undertaken by the other side which actually kind of reinforce this propaganda. And I think a general atmosphere of fear is created which makes it easier for leaders to galvanise support and ensure maybe the support of their people and, again based on the material I reviewed, there is a general fear among many Serbs in Croatia that an independent Croatia would be a repetition of what was witnessed during the Second World War with the Independent State of Croatia, where significant crimes were committed against the Serbs. This was exploited by propaganda on the Serbian side as there was propaganda on the Croatian side and people are influenced by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, the second bullet here, I'm not going to go through all of them, but the second bullet is related to the pulling out of JNA garrisons from Croatia. Was anything in particular happening with respect to the JNA garrisons in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: This is somewhat outside the scope of the report, but in the course of summer and I think predominantly in September 1991, the Croats start with the almost general blockade of JNA barracks and garrisons in Croatia -- I mean, in the areas where there's a Croatian majority. And of course there is a double agenda behind that. Of course the JNA wants to withdraw these garrisons because there's people there, there's equipment and weapons there, and also as we see later there is an attempt to concentrate JNA elements - and at that time the JNA is still a multi-ethnic force, even if there is a lack of response to mobilisations and call-ups mainly by non-Serbs but also by Serbs - the JNA wants to concentrate these forces in safer locations, i.e., areas where there's a larger presence of Serbian citizens in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, at page 141 of your report you make a reference to a letter that Kadijevic writes on the 3rd of October to the citizens of Yugoslavia. This is -- if we can display it on the screen, actually, it's 65 ter 369 at tab 100. Yes. Now, you see this is a similar type of bulletin as the one we saw earlier from the secretary for National Defence, Federal Secretary for National Defence. The date is the 5th of October, and I would like to take you to page 3 I believe in both versions. Yes, if we can zoom on the central part of that page. Thank you. Yes. Now, you see here citizens of Yugoslavia, members of the armed forces of Yugoslavia. The title is: "Statement of the SSNO general army, Veljko Kadijevic." If we scroll -- well, if we go to the next page in both versions, yes, and zoom in to the middle of the page in the English version, please. The perhaps fifth or sixth paragraph which starts with: "Acting upon the decision of the SFRY Presidency ..." Have you located that, Mr. Theunens?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yes, in the middle. It's where the cursor is now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yeah. So: "Acting upon the decision of the SFRY Presidency, our exclusive goal was to prevent bloody inter-ethnic clashes and the repetition of the genocide against the Serbian people ..." And if we scroll down a little bit there's another paragraph -- well, two paragraphs down: "The army now wants nothing more but to restore control in the crisis areas, to protect the Serbian population from persecution and annihilation, and to liberate the army personnel and members of their families." Now, again, with respect to the mission of the JNA, how do you interpret this letter issued on the 3rd of October, 1991?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the mission has obviously changed, but I would -- I mean, in all fairness to Mr. Kadijevic, it's not just -- or anybody else involved in the process, it's not just their own decision but they're also kind of forced by the events. There is no external enemy, but the JNA is being used to -- is used as a force -- as an interposition force to separate armed groups which makes perfect sense. But of course when you dig a bit deeper in this document, the -- I think it illustrates what I said earlier, the use of terminology like genocide and Ustasha and extermination or neo-Naziism and not -- things like neo-Naziism, well, in Croatian documents the use of terms like "Chetnik" is not really conducive to a kind of confidence-building between the various people, and then on the contrary, so it deepens the gap and it actually increases the clout and the authority of people who are pursuing other goals, if I can express myself that way, and I would go more in the direction of the instructions -- what I called the de facto Supreme Command gives to the JNA. And then we end up in a situation that the JNA transfers -- or transforms from being an interposing force or interposition force into a force that is operating in order to liberate between brackets, areas considered Serb, having under its command also groups like paramilitary groups who essentially pursue a purely nationalistic agenda.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. And on page 147 you conclude on this section of your report and you state that JNA ceases to be the SFRY armed forces at least in Croatia and gradually develops into a mainly Serb force; is that right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yes, and maybe one element I haven't mentioned yet, that is of course that -- and again this is something I didn't analyse, but anyone who is slightly familiar with the history will understand. There is -- the non-Serbs or non-Montenegrins are more and more critical towards the JNA and especially in Croatia. I mean, I'm not even mentioning Slovenia anymore, but in Croatia conscripts don't respond anymore to call-ups and there is at the same time an effort to establish Croatian forces with the ZNG and transform Croatian -- I mean, units of the TO which are dominated by Croats in Croatia are then transformed into ZNG and local Serbs transformed their units into their TO units or areas where they take control into their own TO units.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Well, on this topic of the conscripts not responding anymore to call-ups, I'll take you through the next page, 148, where you start dealing with the issue of Serbian volunteers. Now, you describe here - this is page 148 and the B/C/S version is page 181, 182 - you describe the role played by the volunteers during the conflict in Croatia to, as you say, replenish the ranks of the JNA. The first thing that we have is, again, Veljko Kadijevic's position where at least in appearance he seems to - and this is on page 149 - concede the negative impact of some of these volunteer units. Perhaps you could explain to us at this time how the concept of volunteer units comes about in the conflict in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, you mean how they are established or how --

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: -- how they become involved? Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yeah, I mean, this is in the following pages. For -- the Serbs are concerned in the Republic of Serbia various political parties, but these are mainly nationalistic parties, develop their own armed groups. And these groups are apparently tolerated by the authorities, notwithstanding the existing legislation. And these groups, they -- groups, they may recruit volunteers which are then incorporated in existing JNA units or TOs which would still be kind of acceptable, I mean acceptable in the framework of the legislation. But actually what we see is that these groups as such go to Croatia and participate in the fighting. We have seen Dusan Silni earlier. And in the field then efforts are undertaken to subordinate these groups to the JNA in order to implement and to ensure the implementation of the principles of command and control. And what is important in the context of this report is that these groups consist mainly or largely of able men who should actually have joined the military because there were call-ups but they didn't do so because they prefer to fight for political agenda. I mean, there are examples that they are even suspicious of the JNA because they see the JNA as communist whereas, for example, SRS volunteers see themselves first and foremost as nationalists, whereby religion plays also a role and they reject communist. And as we see from the documents these groups, given their motivation and also their composition, often becoming involved in criminal behaviour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, you just said a moment ago that these troops were or these units were tolerated by the authority notwithstanding the legislation. What did the legislation provide with respect to volunteers?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Maybe if you allow me I can give a double answer. We saw Article 118 of the Law on Defence which states that only the government, only the authorities, and this is the Law on Defence of the Republic of Serbia, only authorities are allowed to organise, establish, and train armed forces. And then for what it's worth, whatever I will never forget, the first trial I testified in was the trial of Mr. Milosevic, and I think this was in 2002 or 2003, he said: Well, you know, all these groups were the opposition, they were not the government. But then my answer was: Well, if they were all belonging to the opposition it should have been more of a concern because these groups, you have private groups driven by political motives and they have a military -- they develop military capabilities, they could also be a threat for state security. So actually, the incentive for the Serbian authorities to act against them should actually have been even bigger if, indeed, as Mr. Milosevic claimed in 2002/2003 that they were all belonging to the opposition. So he didn't -- I mean, my understanding was he didn't challenge the fact that they existed, but he tried to explain: Well, you know, they were all belonging to the opposition, it was not the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Perhaps there's a second aspect of this -- of your response here as to what was provided by the legislation with respect to the volunteers?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: I mean, once these groups are there and they are tolerated because nobody acts against them, then we see - and again this is also discussed in the report - measures are taken to -- for example, to compensate members of volunteer groups -- I mean on the level of Serbia they are given certain favours or also entitlements. And then on the level of SFRY and the -- I mean, the armed forces as well as the SFRY or what remains of the SFRY then, decisions are adopted to what I would call legalise their existence and the most obvious example is the SFRY Presidency order number 73 of December 1991, I think -- I mean, I forget the exact name but it's on the participation I think of volunteers -- sorry, on the engagement, I'm sorry, of volunteers in the SFRY armed forces during an imminent threat of war and this is from the 10th of December, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, on page 150 I believe you provide the SSNO's own assessment with respect to the volunteers. And perhaps we could look at this document, it is 65 ter 532 at tab 148, please. Yes, thank you. This is a document of the 7th of November, 1991, and -- yes, we see here that it's a periodical operations report of the OB GMTbr and it's submitted to the SSNO's security administration. Could you just quickly remind us what is the OB GMTbr?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: So, this is drafted by the security organs of the Guards Motorised Brigade, and I mean security organs -- the other name is assistant commander or the chief of the security organs in a brigade is also an assistant commander for security.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And this O -- well, the Guards Motorised Brigade on the 7th of November, 1991, could you tell the Trial Chamber where they were located at the time?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Almost all of the Guards Brigade, I think one battalion stayed in Belgrade, but otherwise almost all of the Guards Brigade is participating in the fighting in the Vukovar area, whereby the command of the Guards Motorised Brigade is also the command of OG South.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, could we go to page 2 on both the English and B/C/S versions. We can zoom in to the middle of the page in the English version. And it's the top of the page in the B/C/S version. Yes. Now, do you see the paragraph or the sentence that begins with: "With regards to the 'Vukovar Operation' ...," where the cursor is right now. The sentence reads that: "... the Serbian nationalistic and the Chetnik propaganda are taking on a serious dimension which, in its breadth, outstrips by far the results in combat of the volunteer groups and the members of the paramilitary units." And the next sentence refers to: "The nationalistic and ideological symbols, the nationalistic songs, the speeches of Seselj, the liquidation of prisoners of war by Chetniks are all unjustifiably tolerated." Now, at this time this is a document written by -- well, this is a report from the security organs that are on the ground. Do you have your own view of when he says tolerated by -- which institutions would be tolerating these instances?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: I mean, there are several of these documents, but it basically shows the complexity of the situation in the sense that the JNA is -- I mean, the JNA officers have been trained to adhere to the values of the SFRY which are totally opposite to the values of people like Chetniks or people calling themselves Ustashas, i.e., nationalistic ideas that, for example, manifested itself during the Second World War in all its negative ways in Yugoslavia. So the JNA has been trained to oppose these kind of ideas and to adhere to the, as I mentioned earlier, the general principle of brotherhood and unity, i.e., equality of all the peoples of Yugoslavia and so on. And of course then they see themselves confronted to an internal conflict and they receive other orders. They start to -- I mean, in -- by November it's clear that the JNA in Vukovar is mainly fighting to, I would say, pursue Serbian goals as I have explained in the report. And at the same time they have -- they see themselves confronted with a lack of manpower because people don't respond to mobilisations, people leave, and so on. And on the other hand you have these volunteers who are eager to fight and they are kind of -- I mean, the JNA in Vukovar -- among, for example, in Vukovar and other areas accept these volunteers even if they -- these volunteers are driven by a different ideology and even, I would say, conflicting ideology compared to that of the JNA. And then you see that instead of, for example, adopting JNA symbols like the red star, these volunteers have their own symbols and have their own kind of doctrine and, as I mentioned, own goals. And security organs in the JNA, again prior to the war this kind of behaviour would have been prohibited and security organs would write about that if such behaviour was shown in the armed forces because it could be a threat against the state. But now in the conflict it's tolerated because the manpower and the drive of these volunteers is needed to achieve the goals, but nevertheless security organs want to express their concern about it because obviously there are negative -- I mean, there are various excesses related to that including what is mentioned here as liquidation of POWs by Chetniks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. The next document that you referred to, Mr. Theunens, at page 151, is a VJ security organ's report. I would like us to display this one on the screen. It is 65 ter 2883, 2883, at tab 446. You indicate in your report that this document is an undated report. First of all, how are you able to assess that this was a VJ security organ's report?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Maybe we have to go in private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, yes --

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Taking into account the origin of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, may we go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Theunens, looking at the first paragraph of this report which appears to be a retrospective report as it starts with: "From the start of the war in 1991, a large number of various paramilitary units and groups were engaged on the territory of the RSK ..." It says here that none of them were completely independent and in various ways they were connected to certain structures in the Republic of Serbia. Do you have any comments in relation to this sentence?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: I can be very brief -- I mean, I can discuss it in detail but then it's going to be very long. What I tried to say is that I looked into this for my report for the Stanisic and Simatovic case, and I mean the relevant documents are also included in the amalgamated report laying in front of us here, that is, that not only were these groups tolerated but some of these groups that were kind of colloquially called volunteers, like Arkan and his Tigers and also Dragan, there is -- I mean, there is extensive documentary material available indicating that they maintained relations with the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Serbia and not only support - I mean materiel support like weapons and ammunition but also that they were allowed to move and were allowed to do the things that they were doing. Just a small aspect in relation when we talk about Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, for these groups, for example, we know that they came from Serbia. To go to Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem obviously they had to come from Serbia and to transit from Baranja to Eastern Slavonia, they had to transit via Serbia, they couldn't move via Croatia. So if the Serbian authorities had any intention to act against these groups, they could have done so because there was Serbian police at the time on the three bridges that separated -- three bridges over the Danube that separated Serbia from Baranja or Eastern Slavonia and Western Srem.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. With respect to that part of your answer here it says that these units and groups lingered longest on the territory of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem. However, when the provisions of the Dayton Agreement came into effect requiring the disengagement of military forces, paramilitary units and groups were also forced to withdraw from this territory. Have you seen documents or do you have information as to how it is that these units lingered longest in this territory?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: I mean the obvious reason is that this territory remained under Serbian control -- I mean, we are talking about Croatia, and this territory remained under Serbian control until the course of 1997, 1998, I'm not sure anymore, but basically the mission -- I served the UNTAES mission, which was United Nations Transitional Administration for Eastern Slavonia. This was a follow-up mission for UNPROFOR because as a result of Operation Storm, Oluja, conducted by the Croatian armed forces or the HV in August 1995, only the eastern part of Croatia remained under Serbian control.
